    Sprint 3 – Moving From Basic To Agentic RAG

    📄

    Model Context Protocol (MCP)

    Lesson 4

    A major challenge in building AI-powered agents, especially those using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques is how to provide consistent, rich context to language models without building custom integrations for every data source or tool. Traditionally, agentic systems have tackled this by injecting retrieved documents, tool outputs, and memory into prompt text. The problem - each new data connector or tool integration has historically been a one-off effort, leading to fragmented solutions that are hard to maintain.


    The Model Context Protocol (MCP) was created to address these issues. MCP provides a universal standard for connecting AI models to the external world of data and capabilities. It is often described as a “USB-C port for AI applications” -  a single, standardized interface through which any compliant AI agent can access any compliant data source or tool. By introducing a common protocol, MCP transforms the integration problem from N×M (every model needs custom code for every tool or dataset) into a much simpler N+M scenario, where each model and each tool only needs to implement MCP once. In practical terms, this means AI systems can easily plug into new information repositories, business applications, or services without additional glue code for each case.


    Crucially, MCP exists in the context of agentic RAG systems to bridge the gap between language models and the up-to-date, domain-specific knowledge they often lack. MCP enables real-time, two-way connections between models and external data sources, so an AI assistant can draw on current facts, search internal knowledge bases, or query APIs on the fly. 


    Finally, the purpose of MCP is not just to feed data to models, but to support the creation of more sophisticated, autonomous agents. Traditional single-turn Q&A bots are limited - truly agentic systems perform multi-step reasoning, call tools, remember past interactions, and proactively complete complex tasks. MCP facilitates this by maintaining a structured context across interactions and tools, so an AI agent can plan and act with continuity. The protocol was explicitly designed to support building “agentic systems” that offload mechanical work to AI, freeing humans to focus on creative aspects. In summary, MCP came to be to provide a strong backbone for context in AI systems - one that standardizes how memories, tools, and goals are represented and shared with models.



    MCP Architecture


    MCP introduces a clean client-server architecture that decouples an AI agent’s core reasoning (the “brain”) from the external data/tool sources it needs to interact with. In a typical MCP deployment there are three roles:


    1. Host Process (Agent Environment): The host is the main AI application or agent container - for example, an IDE plugin, a chatbot interface (in our Amazon shopping assistant case). This is where the user interacts and where the language model is invoked. The host is responsible for orchestrating the agent’s overall workflow and managing connections to various external resources via MCP.

    2. MCP Client: For each external data source or tool, the host spawns a lightweight MCP client module. Each MCP client handles communication with one MCP server, maintaining a dedicated 1:1 connection. The client is like an adapter - it speaks the MCP protocol and ensures that interactions with the server remain isolated and secure (sandboxed) from the rest of the system. The host may run multiple MCP clients simultaneously (one per server) to integrate multiple sources of context.

    3. MCP Server: An MCP server is a program (which can run locally or remotely) that implements the MCP specification to expose some set of capabilities or data. Each server typically connects to a particular data source, knowledge base, or external service, and provides that content or functionality to the host via the standardized protocol. For example, one server might interface with a company’s Google Drive, another with a vector database. An MCP server exposes its capabilities in three main forms: resources (readable data content), tools (executable functions/actions), and prompts (pre-defined prompt templates or system messages). Importantly, servers are stateless about the conversation and focused on their domain - they don’t run the language model themselves, but supply context and actions to whichever model the host (agent) is running.


    The above are used to connect your agents to:


    1. Local Data Sources: Your computer’s files, databases, and services that MCP servers can securely access.

    2. Remote Data Sources: External systems available over the internet (e.g., through APIs) that MCP servers can connect to.


    This architecture cleanly separates concerns. The host/agent focuses on higher-level reasoning and decision-making, while servers focus on providing domain-specific knowledge or actions. The MCP clients in between ensure that communication follows the protocol and that each server remains isolated. This means a server only ever sees the minimal information it needs for its function - it does not get to read the entire conversation or additional context the agent has. The host takes care of all information flow, enforcing security and privacy. For example, if the agent wants to query an internal database via an MCP server, the host can require user consent and then send the query to that server, but the server wouldn’t see unrelated parts of the user’s query or other data sources content. Such isolation is crucial for security and for avoiding unintended coupling between systems.


    Communication between MCP clients and servers is implemented with stateful JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over a chosen transport. For local servers, a simple stdio (pipe) connection can be used, for remote servers, a secure HTTP(S) channel or even server-sent events (SSE) may be employed. The JSON-RPC protocol means every interaction is a structured message - either a Request (from client to server, asking for something like reading a file or executing a tool), a Response/Result (the answer to a request), or a Notification (one-way message like an update or event). This formal messaging layer makes it much easier to manage multi-step dialogues between agent and server. It also allows for features like capability negotiation when a connection initializes - the server advertises what features (resources, tools, etc.) it supports, and the client can advertise if it supports things like server-initiated calls (e.g. sampling requests, which allow the server to ask the model something).


    From a systems-engineering perspective, the benefits of this decoupled architecture are significant. Because servers are lightweight and focused, they are easy to build and maintain for specific needs. An organization could have one team writing an MCP server for their Confluence wiki, another building a server for their JIRA tickets, another for inventory data in stock. Each server is independent and can evolve or scale on its own, as long as it speaks MCP. Meanwhile, the host application (agent) remains general: it just knows how to load an MCP client and connect, without hard-coding any one integration. This modular design means new integrations become “plug-and-play” - instead of writing new parsing logic or prompts, a developer can stand up a new MCP server or reuse an open-source one, and immediately the agent can talk to that new data source through the standard interface. The host also aggregates context from multiple servers as needed, effectively merging the contributions into the model’s context window in a structured way. Because MCP connections are stateful, the agent can subscribe to updates (e.g. a server can notify when a file changed) and maintain a persistent memory of resources throughout a task, rather than forgetting everything each turn. Overall, MCP’s client-server setup enforces clear separation of concerns - each component can be developed, scaled, and secured independently - which leads to a more modular, scalable AI system design.



    Structuring Model Context with MCP


    One of MCP’s core contributions is a formal structure for model context. Instead of injecting arbitrary text into a prompt, MCP defines standard data structures to represent the various pieces of context an agent might need - such as long-term memories, current goals, available tools, interim observations, and even system instructions. This structured approach makes context portable and machine-readable, allowing different agent frameworks to share and reuse context more easily. Let’s break down some of the key MCP concepts and how they map to those familiar agent components:


    • Resources: In MCP, resources refer to read-only contextual data that servers can expose to the client (and thereby to the AI model). A resource might be a file, a database entry, a document, or any piece of information that provides context for reasoning. Each resource is identified by a URI and can be listed and fetched via the MCP protocol (using resources/list and resources/read calls). In simpler terms, resources are structured knowledge or data that an agent can retrieve on demand. Because they are structured and addressable, resources can be searched, indexed, and fetched systematically rather than dumped into a prompt. They remain separate from the agent's dialogue but can be injected when needed. They are strictly observational (no side effects), which ensures that pulling in a resource doesn't alter anything in the environment - it just provides information.

    • Tools and Tool Descriptions: Tools are first-class citizens in MCP. An MCP server can advertise any number of tools (functions) that the AI model can invoke, each described with metadata. This includes a human-readable description of what the tool does, the function signature or schema for its arguments and return value, and possibly annotations like cost, rate limits, or expected latency. By standardizing tool metadata, MCP allows agents to reason about tools in a uniform way - for instance, the agent can decide not just which tool to use, but also consider when or how to use it based on the provided metadata (like avoiding a slow tool if a faster one is available). In a traditional approach, an agent developer might hard-code tool usage with prompts or rely on vendor-specific function calling. In MCP, tools are exposed via the protocol and invoked through JSON-RPC requests (tools/call messages), making the process model-agnostic and decoupled from any single LLM vendor’s API. Tools can range from simple utilities (e.g. a calculator) to complex actions (e.g. executing a database query or calling an external API). MCP essentially provides a unified interface to all tools, so that integrating a new tool is as simple as running or connecting a new server, rather than changing the agent’s code. All the usage instructions for tools can be provided in the structured tool description and related system message.

    • System Messages and Prompts: MCP also formalizes how system instructions or prompt templates are provided to the model. An MCP server can supply prompts, which are basically reusable message templates or workflow scripts that can guide the model or user. For example, a server might have a prompt template for a certain task domain. System messages - the instructions that define the agent’s role, tone, or high-level behavior - can be considered part of this contextual prompt material. In many agent setups, system messages include a description of the agent’s persona and available tools. With MCP, such instructions can be delivered in a structured way or fetched from a server when needed. The benefit is consistency: every time an agent engages in a task, it can pull the appropriate system instructions or templates from an MCP server. MCP prompts feature consequently helps avoid hard-coding system messages into the agent code, instead they can be treated as data, managed and versioned on the server side.

    • Context Objects: In MCP, a context object serves as a container for the agent’s state and knowledge related to the task at hand. It encapsulates things like the agent’s memory (e.g. facts or data brought in from prior interactions or retrieved from knowledge bases), the task state or goals (what the agent is currently trying to achieve), the tool descriptions (details of what tools/functions are available), and any prior observations (results from previous actions or environment feedback). Think of the context object as the structured equivalent of what would otherwise be a long system or prompt message containing all this information. Because it’s structured (often in JSON form), an MCP context can be saved, versioned, or transmitted between systems without losing meaning. For example, rather than a free-text summary of “what the agent knows so far”, the context object might have distinct fields for relevant documents, for intermediate conclusions drawn, and for the tools at the agent’s disposal with their usage instructions. This makes the context both comprehensive and machine-parseable.

    • Task and Goal Representation: In an agentic context, the task (or goal) the agent is working on is a critical piece of context. MCP doesn’t prescribe a specific “task object”, but the task state can be part of the context object or exchanged via the protocol. For instance, a host might send the server a brief description of the user’s query or the agent’s current goal when initializing a session, so the server knows the context of what’s being asked. Conversely, a server might offer prompt templates or resources keyed to certain task types.

    • Observations: In agent loops, observations are the feedback an agent gets after performing an action. This could be the result of a tool call (e.g. the output of a web search) or an environmental change. MCP captures observations as part of the structured context so they can be remembered and referenced. For example, if an agent used a “web search” MCP server to fetch information, the result might come back as a resource or message that is then stored in the context object as a prior observation. This way, the agent’s subsequent reasoning can explicitly include “Observation: (the data retrieved)”. By logging observations in a structured way, MCP enables a clearer chain-of-thought trace. In fact, MCP-based systems naturally produce logs of the thought -> action -> observation loop, since each tool invocation and result is a JSON event. These structured traces can be used for debugging or even fine-tuning later. In short, observations are no longer ephemeral pieces of text but become part of the agent’s state that can be analyzed and shared across components.

    • Invocation Metadata: Another concept defined in MCP is invocation metadata - essentially metadata about calling models or tools. This includes details like the API or model being invoked, expected latency or cost of that call, and how to format the output. For example, if the agent is about to call an LLM for a completion, invocation metadata might specify which model engine to use, any time/compute budget, or the format (e.g. “JSON response expected”). Similarly, for tool functions, the metadata could note if the tool call is expensive or should be rate-limited. By exposing such details, MCP allows the agent (or the host application) to make smarter decisions - e.g. routing a request to a cheaper model if the expensive one isn’t necessary, or deciding not to call a tool if its latency is too high for an interactive session. It also helps in model-agnosticism: instead of coding these decisions per vendor, the agent can rely on metadata. Model descriptors fall in a similar vein: they describe what type of model or agent is on the other end (is it a text-only LLM, a vision model expecting an image, etc.) so that the system can route requests to the appropriate model or modality. All these pieces (descriptors, invocation metadata, routing info) make up a sort of “overhead” context that guides how and where the actual AI reasoning is executed. In a layered view, if the context objects carry the content (the what), the invocation metadata and routing information carry the logistics of execution (the how and where). MCP formalizes this logistic layer too, which is crucial for building complex systems that might involve multiple models or fallback strategies.



    Splitting control responsibilities.


    • Prompts are designed to be User-Controlled: Programmer of the server can expose specific prompts (suited for interaction with data exposed by the server) that can be injected into the application using LLMs and exposed to the user of the given application.

    • Resources are designed to be Application-Controlled: Resources are any kind of data (text or binary) that can be used by the application built to utilise LLMs. The programmer of the application (usually AI Engineer) is responsible of codifying how this information should be used by the application. Usually, there is not automation in that and LLM does not participate in this choice.

    • Tools are designed to be Model-Controlled: If we provide agency to our application of how it should interact with the environment we use tools to do that. MCP Server exposes an endpoint that can list all of the tools available with their descriptions and required arguments, application can pass this list to the LLM so that it can decide which tools are needed for the task at hand and how they should be invoked.


    By structuring everything from factual context to tools, goals, and execution metadata in a declarative, JSON-based format, MCP makes context consistent and shareable across the AI ecosystem. Because MCP is model-agnostic, these context packages can be used with any LLM or even multi-modal models without losing meaning. In general, MCP defines a universal context language for AI agents - one that any compliant agent can understand, regardless of the underlying framework. This is why MCP can serve as the “context layer” in a layered AI architecture, analogous to how TCP/IP serves as a networking layer - it abstracts how context is packaged and exchanged, allowing higher-level agent logic (application layer) and lower-level model execution (model layer) to remain decoupled.



    Using MCP to Integrate RAG, Memory and Tools


    For practitioners in AI engineering, one of the most exciting aspects of MCP is how it allows the integration of retrieval-augmented generation, long-term memory and tool use under one consistent interface. In a traditional setup, each of these capabilities might involve separate modules or libraries - for example, a RAG pipeline to fetch documents, an in-memory vector store for “memory”, a set of API wrappers for tools and custom code to orchestrate reasoning. With MCP, these can all be plugged into the agent through the same standardized mechanism, simplifying development.


    Consider a concrete scenario: you are building an AI assistant that can answer customer questions by looking up internal inventory data (classic RAG), can perform actions like updating shopping cart (tool use), and can remember the conversation or user preferences over time (long-term memory). Using MCP, you could set up three servers: (1) a Inventory MCP server that exposes inventory knowledge base as searchable resources, (2) a Shopping Cart MCP server that provides a “addItem” tool function, and (3) a Memory MCP server that stores and retrieves conversational memory or user profile info. Your agent (the host process) connects to all three. Now, when a user asks a question, the agent can query the Inventory server for relevant text (perhaps via a resources/search request, in most cases you still use tools for this) and get back a snippet or item ID, it can also retrieve any relevant user info from the Memory server. All that data comes back as structured JSON, which the host can then insert into the model’s context in a controlled way (for example, by constructing a prompt with the returned document text). If the user’s request requires an action (“please add the third earphones to the shopping cart”), the agent can call the Shopping Cart server’s tool through a tools/call message, passing the necessary details. The result of that action (update ID, confirmation, etc.) is returned and can be used to formulate the final answer to the user. Throughout this process, the agent interacts with all external systems through a uniform API (MCP) - it doesn’t need to know the details of the Shopping Cart API underneath or how memory is stored, it simply makes high-level requests like ListResources or CallTool and gets back JSON results. This reduces the cognitive load on the agent developer - you can integrate new capabilities by following the same pattern each time.


    This is how tool calling procedure via MCP is different compared to regular function calling:


    1. User Query is passed to the Agent (usually a Python application).

    2. The application implements MCP Client and via it retrieves all available tools from the MCP servers.

    3. The list of available Tools is passed together with the User Query to a LLM via a prompt. The LLM figures out which tools need to be invoked and with what parameters.

    4. The Agent application communicates with the MCP server (via MCP Client) again and sends the tool execution request. After execution completes the Agent receives the required data.

    5. User Query is sent to the LLM together with the data retrieved by the Tool calls.

    6. The answer is constructed and returned to the user via the Agent.


    Moreover, MCP encourages a more interactive style of RAG and tool use. Traditional RAG might do a single retrieval step before generating an answer. In MCP, because servers maintain a session and can even send notifications, the agent can engage in multi-turn retrieval or tool use. For example, an MCP server could push updates or ask clarifying questions back to the agent if a query is ambiguous. Or an agent could subscribe to a resource and get notified if it changes while the task is ongoing. This opens the door for agents that are deeply integrated into their environment, not just static one-shot retrievers.


    Looking back into the diagram of a fully-fleshed out Agentic RAG, this is how it would look like with MCP in the picture:


    1. Analysis of the user query: we pass the original user query to a LLM based Agent for analysis. This is where:

      • The original query can be rewritten, sometimes multiple times to create either a single or multiple queries to be passed down the pipeline.

      • The agent decides if additional data sources are required to answer the query.

    2. If additional data is required, the Retrieval step is triggered. We could tap into variety of data types, few examples:

      • Real time user data.

      • Internal documents that a user might be interested in.

      • Data available on the web.


    This is also where MCP comes into the game:


    • Each data domain can manage their own MCP Servers. Exposing specific rules of how the data should be used.

    • Security and compliance can be ensured on the Servel level for each domain.

    • New data domains can be easily added to the MCP server pool in a standardised way with no Agent rewrite needed enabling decoupled evolution of the system.

    • Platform builders can expose their data in a standardised way to external consumers. Enabling easy access to data on the web.

    • AI Engineers can continue to focus on the topology of the Agent.


    1. Retrieved data is consolidated and Reranked by a more powerful model compared to regular embedder. Data points are significantly narrowed down.

    2. If there is no need for additional data, we try to compose the answer (or multiple answers or a set of actions) straight via an LLM.

    3. The answer gets analyzed, summarized and evaluated for correctness and relevance:

      • If the Agent decides that the answer is good enough, it gets returned to the user.

      • If the Agent decides that the answer needs improvement, we try to rewrite the user query and repeat the generation loop.


    Integration of memory is also enhanced. An MCP memory server might interface with a vector database or other storage, but to the agent it looks like just another resource provider (this is also similar to what interacting with Mem0 would look like). Agents can offload long-term memory to such a server, which can then feed relevant memory chunks back when needed. Because the memory is externalized, it’s not limited by the model’s context window alone, the agent can fetch more when needed, and the memory can persist across sessions. One of MCP’s advantages is the ability to have persistent context that spans sessions or is shared between agents. For example, if Agent A solves part of a task and Agent B continues it later, they could both utilize the same MCP-accessible memory repository to store and read what has been done. This continuity is hard to achieve with ad-hoc methods, but straightforward with MCP as the interface to a shared memory store. When it comes to agent reasoning, MCP doesn’t replace the agent’s internal logic (e.g. planning and deciding when to use a tool), but it provides the scaffolding that makes such reasoning more effective. Agents built on MCP can follow the Thought -> Action -> Observation loop in a very natural way: the “Thought” can be a step where the agent considers the available MCP-provided context and decides on an action, the “Action” is executed by making an MCP request (like calling a tool or reading a resource), the resulting “Observation” comes back as a structured response which the agent then incorporates into its next Thought. Because all observations come in a normalized format (rather than arbitrary text from different APIs), the agent can learn patterns to interpret and use them effectively. For example, if a tool returns an error or a specific result schema, the agent can be prepared (via prompt or fine-tuning) to recognize that structure and adjust its plan accordingly. This consistency in formatting is critical for context engineering and for the agent’s reliability. Additionally, since MCP can log every request and result, developers get a clear trace of the agent’s reasoning chain, which can be visualized or analyzed to improve the prompts or fix failure points.


    From a developer’s perspective, using MCP means learning one API paradigm and applying it everywhere. Anthropic provides SDKs (in Python, TypeScript, etc.) that handle much of the request/response handling for MCP, making it quite straightforward to implement both servers and clients. For instance, if you want to integrate a new web service into your agent (we’ll do that for our search capabilities), you can create a small MCP server for it (leveraging an SDK) that defines some resources or tools for that service. Your agent can then start using it immediately, and if you’ve adhered to MCP’s spec, any other agent could as well. This also means that integrating things like retrieval augmentation becomes less about writing custom logic and more about configuration, e.g. pointing to a pre-built “Inventory MCP server” when you want to know about the available items in stock. Also, the ecosystem already includes servers for common needs: web search, note-taking apps (Obsidian, Notion), various cloud APIs, code repositories, and more. Developers can mix and match these to assemble the capabilities required for a given project. The result is a consistent interface across various functionalities: your code to call a database looks the same as your code to trigger a web scrape, aside from different method names or parameters.


    By using MCP as the connective tissue, you can focus on agent logic and strategy rather than low-level integration details. The agent’s design can implement MCP for things like retrieving the right context (instead of manually managing vector index queries), executing actions (instead of writing individual API calls and parsing their responses), and maintaining state (instead of threading state through prompts). As your needs grow (say you incorporate a new modality like an image model, or a new knowledge source), you can extend the system by adding new MCP endpoints without refactoring the core agent. With MCP, the integration of RAG, memory, and tool use becomes a configuration detail, and the agent developer can concentrate on higher-level behaviors and ensure the model is using the provided context effectively.



    Real-World Adoption and Examples


    MCP may be relatively new (open-sourced in late 2024 by Anthropic), but it’s already seeing wide adoption in a variety of real-world projects. Several forward-looking companies and open-source contributors have integrated MCP into their AI stacks:


    • Developer Tools Integration: Developer productivity AI has been a big early use case. For example, Sourcegraph’s Cody (an AI coding assistant) uses MCP to interface with large codebases and documentation, allowing it to fetch relevant code context on demand and provide more accurate suggestions to developers. Zed, a collaborative code editor, has incorporated MCP so that its AI features can talk to development tools and repositories seamlessly. These integrations enable an AI coding agent to, e.g. retrieve the content of a file or get the diff of a pull request via an MCP server, then reason about it to generate code or reviews.

    • Enterprise Knowledge Assistants: Companies are also exploring MCP for internal knowledge management. Anthropic has mentioned early adopters like Block (formerly Square) and Apollo who integrated MCP to connect AI assistants with their internal systems. By doing so, an internal AI assistant can securely access things like policy documents, databases or Slack discussions through MCP servers, all with the organization retaining control. This indicates a belief that MCP will underpin the next generation of enterprise AI, where transparency and collaboration (across tools and teams) are essential.

    • Web and Data Agents: MCP has been used to give AI agents capabilities like browsing and data extraction. For instance, Apify, known for web scraping automation, developed an MCP server that exposes all of Apify’s web scraping actors to AI agents. This means an agent can, via MCP, instruct Apify to scrape a website or gather data, then get the results back to analyze or present - effectively blending RAG with web automation. Similarly, there are MCP connectors for web search that let an AI agent perform internet queries for real-time information. By plugging in a “web search” MCP server, any agent (regardless of which LLM it uses) can gain internet access in a controlled way. Another example is connecting to note-taking applications like Notion or Obsidian via MCP servers, enabling an AI assistant to read and update a user’s notes or knowledge base on command.

    • Research Applications: Some projects use MCP in experimental multi-agent systems. For example, there are efforts to benchmark agent abilities (like the MCPWorld benchmark on API, GUI tasks) which rely on MCP as the interface for agents to perform tasks in various environments. This highlights MCP's role in academic and R&D contexts as a way to compare agent strategies in the same environment. By having a standardized testbed (MCP servers representing tasks or tools), researchers can swap out the agent's reasoning engine and fairly evaluate outcomes - something much harder to do when every agent is wired up differently.


    It’s worth noting that an open-source ecosystem is growing around MCP. Anthropic provided an initial set of SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Java, etc.) and a repository of example servers (for Google Drive, Git, Slack, PostgreSQL, and more). The community has been contributing connectors for additional services, often sharing them via GitHub or a registry (Anthropic’s Smithery, for instance, is a gallery of community-contributed MCP servers). This means that if you have a need - e.g. connecting to a calendar or a CRM - it’s possible someone has already built an MCP server for it, or at least a template to start from. The collaborative nature of MCP’s development (with a formal spec and discussion forums for improvements) suggests it’s meant to be a long-term standard, not a transient library.
